REC LIMITED : SUCCESSFULLY ISSUED INDIA'S FIRST PILOT ISSUE ON TOKENIZED CORPORATE BONDS UNDER SEBI REGULATORY SANDBOX FRAMEWORK

• REC Limited successfully issued India's First Pilot Issue on Tokenized Corporate Bonds under SEBI Regulatory Sandbox Framework.
• The size of pilot issue was ₹500 Crore (base issue of ₹100 Crore with a green shoe option of ₹400 Crore) and bidding was undertaken at EBP platform of National Stock Exchange of India Limited (NSE).
• The issue received an overwhelming market response from investors, clocking a book building of ₹796 Crore (oversubscribed by ~8x).
• REC has accepted ₹500 Crore at a coupon rate of 7.30% per annum for a tenor of 1 year 9 months.
• The tokenised mode enabled faster settlement, with pay-in, allotment and listing of the bonds on same day.
• The bonds are listed on NSE and BSE Limited.
Impact: Positive (Landmark issuance of India's first tokenized corporate bonds under SEBI sandbox framework)

HFCL FY26 Annual Report Key Takeaways 🧵

• Strong FY26: Revenue grew 21.8% to ₹4,949 Cr, EBITDA +63.2% to ₹827 Cr and PAT +90.1% to ₹329 Cr.

• Margins expanding: EBITDA margin improved sharply to 16.7% from 12.5%, driven by better product mix and higher capacity utilisation.

• Business mix changing: Product-led revenue rose to 62% from 42%, while private customers increased to 84% from 65%.

• Exports taking off: Export contribution jumped to 41.4% from 12.2% in FY25, with >70% of cable production now serving international markets.

• Big global win: ₹10,159 Cr ($1.1B) OFC (Optical Fiber Cable) supply agreement with a global hyperscaler. Management targets exports at >50% of revenue by FY27.

• Strong visibility: Order book stood at ₹21,206 Cr in March 2026 and increased to ₹26,665 Cr by June 2026.

• Profitability is shifting: Telecom Products generated ₹2,931 Cr revenue and ₹764 Cr segment profit, while Turnkey Contracts generated ₹1,875 Cr revenue but a ₹113 Cr loss.

• Strategic pivot working: HFCL is moving from lower-margin project execution towards higher-margin, product-led businesses.

• Capacity expansion: OF capacity targeted at 38.5 mn fkm (fiber kilometer) and OFC capacity at 56.36 mn fkm by July 2028, with ~₹580 Cr being invested in backward integration into preforms.

• Defence opportunity: Defence revenue targeted at ₹500 Cr in FY27 vs ₹77 Cr in FY26, with a ~₹2,189 Cr defence/aerospace pipeline.

• Aerospace entry: Proposed acquisition brings an export-oriented ₹1,890 Cr order book, while a 1,000-acre defence facility is being developed in Andhra Pradesh.

• BharatNet optionality: HFCL has secured >₹7,335 Cr of Phase III contracts and sees upcoming opportunities worth >₹50,000 Cr.

• R&D focus: 229 R&D professionals are working across 5G, Wi-Fi, AI-enabled networking and emerging 6G technologies.

• Balance sheet: Debt increased to ₹1,713 Cr, but Net Debt/Equity remained comfortable at 0.34x.

• Key concern - cash flow: Operating cash flow was -₹335 Cr despite ₹329 Cr PAT, mainly due to higher inventory and receivables supporting the growing order book.

Overall, FY26 marks a meaningful transformation - from projects to products, domestic to global, and telecom towards a broader connectivity + defence + aerospace platform.

ESDS | AI INFRASTRUCTURE + NEO CLOUD OPTIONALITY

GLOBAL AI INFRA CYCLE
- Global neocloud players are scaling rapidly as AI drives demand for GPU compute, power, cooling, networking, storage and data-centre capacity.
- AI infrastructure is structurally different from the traditional CPU-driven data-centre cycle.
- Training requires massive GPU capacity, while inference could become an even larger recurring compute opportunity as AI adoption expands.
- Data-centre availability is increasingly becoming a bottleneck, with large AI customers securing capacity years in advance.

GLOBAL NEO CLOUD SIGNALS
- Anthropic has signed major AI-compute commitments with Lambda and Nscale.
- CoreWeave has built a massive contracted backlog.
- Nebius has secured large contracts with Microsoft and Meta, alongside Nvidia investment.
- Sharon AI is scaling from hundreds of deployed GPUs toward 64,000+ Nvidia GPUs by mid-2027.
- Nvidia's involvement with neocloud companies highlights the creation of an entire new AI infrastructure layer around GPUs.

ESDS | THE BIG BET
- ESDS has signed for an ~8,200 Nvidia B300 GPU cluster through Sharon AI.
- Contract is worth approximately $1.25 Bn over 5 years on a take-or-pay basis.
- 8,200 B300 GPUs represents a meaningful initial AI-infrastructure deployment rather than a small pilot.
- The key question is whether this becomes the foundation for a much larger GPU/neocloud business.

REVENUE SCALE-UP
- Current estimates indicate potential revenue progression from:
  FY26: ~₹472 Cr → FY27: ~₹2,263 Cr → FY28: ~₹4,581 Cr
- This would represent a dramatic transformation in the company's revenue scale.
- However, the bigger opportunity is replication beyond the currently announced contract.

THE REAL BULL CASE
- First deployment succeeds → economics are proven → additional GPU clusters are added.
- 8,200 GPUs → 20,000 → 30,000+ GPUs could materially change the scale of the business.
- Multiple large contracts with global neocloud players could create rapid operating leverage.
- The strategic advantage would come from having Indian data-centre capacity + execution experience + proven AI infrastructure economics.

PAT OPTIONALITY
- Rough bull-case estimate:
  - FY27 PAT: ~₹400 Cr
  - FY28 PAT: potentially ~₹2,000 Cr
- This is an aggressive personal bull case, not management guidance.
- A ₹2,000 Cr PAT outcome would require substantially more business than currently announced.

VALUATION OPTIONALITY
- At ₹2,000 Cr PAT, a hypothetical ₹1 lakh Cr market cap = ~50× earnings.
- From current levels, that could imply roughly 8–9× upside in ~1.5 years.
- Extremely aggressive scenario, dependent on substantial execution and contract replication.

KEY RISKS
- First 8,200-GPU deployment must be executed successfully.
- GPU economics, utilisation and cash-flow conversion need to be proven.
- The initial $1.25 Bn contract must translate into sustainable earnings rather than remain a one-off opportunity.
- Additional large contracts are essential for the extreme bull case.
- High execution requirements make this a high-risk, high-optionality AI infrastructure thesis.

KEY TAKEAWAY
- The real ESDS thesis is not simply the existing 8,200-GPU contract.
- It is whether that contract becomes the first building block of a scalable Indian neocloud/GPU infrastructure platform.
- Global AI demand is visible. GPU shortages are visible. Data-centre capacity is constrained.
- The critical trigger is now:
  DEPLOY → UTILISE → PROVE ECONOMICS → REPLICATE → SCALE
- If ESDS can successfully move through that cycle, the potential earnings trajectory could look dramatically different from the company's current scale.

Vintage Coffee has proposed a ₹68.88 Cr promoter-led warrant issue

The proposal involves:

• 42 lakh warrants at ₹164 each
• Conversion into equity within 18 months
• Promoter holding rising from 34.65% to 36.49%
• Warrant-only dilution of approximately 2.8%
• A separate ESOP pool of up to 30 lakh options

Why does the timing matter?

Vintage Coffee’s expanded 11,000 MTPA capacity is already operating at around 90–95% utilisation.

Management stated:
“We have received the volume commitments for the whole year, FY27.”

The operating numbers are also scaling:

• Q1 revenue: ₹161 Cr, up 58%
• EBITDA: ₹31.6 Cr, up 75%
• PAT: ₹20.8 Cr, up 46%
• FY27 revenue indication: ₹850–900 Cr

The next leg is the ₹550 Cr freeze-dried coffee plant, which will add 5,500 MTPA and take total capacity to 16,500 MTPA.

However, there is one question investors should ask.

In August, management said:

“As of now, as per the plan, it is not required.”
One month later, warrants and a separate ESOP pool have been proposed.

Promoter participation is reassuring and dilution is modest but clarity on the use of funds and the changed capital plan will be important.

India’s Future Industrial SuperCycle Complete:

👉 India’s next decade is not likely to be defined by one “hot sector”, but by multiple structural themes converging into one industrial ecosystem.
👉 Advanced Materials → Precision Components → Advanced Manufacturing → Semiconductors & Electronics → Power → Machines & Automation → Strategic Systems → Intelligence & AI.

👉 The Second-Order Effect:
  → AI drives demand for compute, semiconductors, power and data centres; machines turn that intelligence into physical action; defence, aerospace, space and maritime convert industrial capability into strategic systems.
  → Every layer pulls demand from the layers beneath it - creating a compounding cycle across materials, components, electronics, manufacturing and infrastructure.
  → The most interesting companies may be those sitting at the intersection of multiple themes, where demand comes from several structural trends rather than a single narrative.

👉 That’s the bigger thesis: India’s future may be built not by isolated industries, but by an interconnected industrial stack where: Materials enable Components → Components enable Manufacturing → Manufacturing enables Systems → Systems create Intelligence → Intelligence accelerates the entire ecosystem.
👉 The opportunity is not just finding the next big theme - it is finding the companies that benefit from several of them at once.

*Our takeaway* 
 
The meeting was encouraging. 
 
The key investment thesis is not simply rising solar demand. It is the combination of: 
 
*High entry barriers in solar glass + strong domestic demand + limited merchant domestic supply + 30–35% potential EBITDA margins + meaningful capacity addition from FY28 + possible policy protection against imports.* 
 
The immediate monitorable is the temporary SG1/SG2 maintenance shutdown and execution of the new furnaces. 
 
Beyond this, *FY28 could potentially represent a meaningful earnings inflection year* as the additional ~600 TPD capacity contributes for a full year and average production moves towards ~1,500 TPD. 
 
The biggest variables to watch remain solar-glass pricing, timing of BIS/QCO implementation, actual domestic competitor additions and execution of Borosil's capacity ramp-up to 2800 TPD.

*BOROSIL RENEWABLES – Management Interaction | Key Takeaways* 
 
Our interaction with Borosil Renewables management reinforced our view that the *solar glass industry is structurally very different from the solar module industry*, with substantially higher capital intensity, longer commissioning timelines and greater operating complexity creating meaningful entry barriers. 
 
*1. Demand outlook remains strong* 
 
Management does *not see any demand challenge* for solar glass. India is currently seeing annual solar module deployment of ~*60–65 GW*, while emerging demand from *data centres, EVs and green hydrogen* is not fully captured in this number. 
 
Management believes that even if industry demand were to fall by *20–30%*, domestic solar-glass capacity should still remain well utilised. 
 
*2. Solar glass has significantly higher entry barriers than modules* 
 
This remains one of the most important takeaways. 
 
A solar module manufacturing facility can be established with only around *₹50–100 crore/GW* of investment and can also be shut relatively quickly. 
 
Solar glass, on the other hand, requires roughly *₹300–350 crore/GW*. A *1,000 TPD glass plant requires ~₹ 2000  crore plus of investment, involves significant fuel consumption and cannot be switched on/off easily. 
 
This should structurally favour established domestic glass manufacturers as the module industry eventually consolidates. 
 
*3. Order environment remains extremely healthy* 
 
Management indicated that most monthly orders are already booked *by around the 10th of the previous month*. 
 
Importantly, demand is currently strong enough that Borosil has the ability to *choose which orders it wants to execute*, rather than chase volumes. 
 
Current solar-glass realisation is around *₹160*, with an additional surcharge of approximately *₹9.5*. 
 
Imported glass also carries the disadvantage of roughly *two months of planning/lead time* along with logistics costs. 
 
*4. 30–35% EBITDA margin indicated for glass* 
 
The glass business delivered approximately *35% EBITDA margin last quarter*. 
 
Management believes a *30–35% EBITDA margin range* is sustainable for the solar-glass business under the present operating environment. 
 
This is important because the next phase of capacity expansion can therefore translate into meaningful operating leverage if pricing remains supportive. 
 
*5. Capacity expansion starts reflecting meaningfully from FY28* 
 
Current solar-glass capacity is approximately *1,000 TPD*, with operating yields of around *69–71%*. 
 
Two additional furnaces are expected to be lit by *March 2027*, with roughly *600 TPD of incremental capacity* beginning to reflect in financial numbers from *April 2027*. 
 
Management indicated average production of around *1,500 TPD for FY28*, which suggests FY28 can be the first full year capturing the benefit of the expanded capacity. 
 
*6. Maintenance will temporarily impact production* 
 
SG1 and SG2 will undergo maintenance for approximately *75 days*. 
 
During this period, around *470 TPD* of capacity will temporarily be unavailable from the expanded ~1,600 TPD base. 
 
We would therefore distinguish between this temporary maintenance impact and the underlying demand/capacity ramp-up story. 
 
*7. Domestic capacity remains significantly short of demand* 
 
Management estimates that even after the currently planned industry expansions, domestic solar-glass manufacturing capacity would meet only around *30–40% of Indian demand*. 
 
This suggests India may continue requiring meaningful imports unless domestic capacities expand substantially. 
 
*8. Competitive capacity may be less threatening than headline announcements suggest* 
 
Management believes *Reliance's solar-glass production is likely to be consumed internally* rather than coming into the merchant market.

**CITI ON GAS CGD SECTOR | SEPTEMBER 07, 2026**

**Key Developments**
• **HP/HT Gas Allocation** – Government has revised the HP/HT gas allocation mechanism for future auctions, which should benefit larger CGDs such as **IGL & MGL**.
• **New Allocation Formula** – HP/HT gas allocation will now be linked to a CGD’s **absolute requirement**, calculated as the shortfall between **CNG + domestic PNG consumption** and its utilisation of **APM + NWG gas** in the preceding quarter.
• **Earlier Methodology** – Previously, available HP/HT gas volumes were distributed equally among eligible bidding CGDs, meaning smaller CGDs could receive the same allocation as much larger players.
• **Benefit to Large CGDs** – The revised methodology better aligns gas allocations with **actual consumption requirements**, potentially improving access to cheaper HP/HT gas for larger CGDs.
• **Margin Support** – Recent **retail price hikes by CGDs** are likely to provide additional support to margins.
• **Medium-Term Outlook** – With improved gas allocation and better pricing, the CGD sector appears well positioned from a **medium-term perspective**.

**Gas Value Chain Pecking Order**
• **MGL > IGL > GAIL > GEL > PLNG**

**Key Takeaway**
• Revised HP/HT gas allocation should structurally favour **large CGDs**, particularly **MGL & IGL**, by aligning allocations with actual gas requirements. Combined with recent retail price hikes, the changes could support **gas availability and margins**, making the sector attractive from a medium-term perspective.

SUNDRAM FASTENERS | NON-AUTO PIVOT

THE STRATEGIC SHIFT
- Sundram Fasteners is gradually shifting revenue away from its core Indian auto OEM fasteners & powertrain parts business.
- Existing book is ~₹6,000 Cr, with significant exposure to domestic auto and ICE powertrain.
- Focus is shifting toward Wind + Aerospace + Railways — engineered, qualification-heavy non-auto businesses.

🌬 WIND | LARGEST NEW VERTICAL
- Current revenue: ₹25–30 Cr/month (~₹350 Cr annualised).
- Management is building capacity toward ₹500 Cr revenue.
- Planned capex: only ~₹100 Cr.
- Existing forging and machining capabilities are being leveraged rather than building an entirely new greenfield setup.

✈️ AEROSPACE | HIGH-VALUE OPTIONALITY
- FY26 revenue: ₹50 Cr.
- FY27 target: ₹100 Cr+.
- 2–3 year target: ~₹500 Cr.
- Qualification-heavy aerospace products can support better economics and create long-term customer relationships.

🚆 RAILWAYS
- Current revenue: ₹2–3 Cr/month.
- Target: ~₹100 Cr annually.
- Adds exposure to railway and infrastructure capex rather than depending solely on automobile demand.

MARGIN EXPANSION
- Wind, aerospace and rail products are typically lower-volume and qualification-heavy.
- Pricing is driven more by engineering value than recurring OEM cost-down pressure.
- Potentially structurally better margins than commodity fasteners supplied to large domestic auto OEMs.

DE-CYCLICALISATION
- Domestic auto remains cyclical, while a significant portion of the existing business is linked to ICE powertrain.
- EV penetration creates a long-term risk for traditional engine-related components.
- Wind and rail are driven by energy/infrastructure capex cycles, while aerospace benefits from multi-year global backlogs.
- This can gradually reduce dependence on the domestic automobile cycle.

CAPITAL EFFICIENCY
- Wind provides a potential ₹500 Cr revenue opportunity against only ~₹100 Cr capex.
- The strategy is to monetise the existing forging, machining and manufacturing base across new end-markets.
- This creates the possibility of strong incremental returns without heavy greenfield investment.

GLOBAL CUSTOMER DIVERSIFICATION
- Wind and aerospace have greater exposure to global OEM customers.
- Higher exports can diversify the revenue base.
- Reduces dependence on a concentrated set of domestic automotive accounts.

KEY TAKEAWAY
- The important story is not just growth in Sundram Fasteners' existing auto business.
- The bigger structural opportunity is the mix shift from commodity/ICE-linked auto components toward higher-value Wind + Aerospace + Railways.
- If execution continues, the company could become less cyclical, more export-oriented and structurally higher-margin over time.

ELANTAS BECK INDIA | ELECTRIFICATION + SPECIALTY CHEMICALS

BUSINESS OVERVIEW
- Makes specialty chemistry that protects electrical equipment — wire enamels, insulating varnishes & resins, casting/potting compounds and electronic materials.
- Applications span motors, transformers, generators, pumps, appliances, automotive electronics, EVs and other electrical systems.
- CY25 revenue mix: Electrical Insulation ~81% | EERM ~19%.

STRONG MOAT & PRICING POWER
- Products are often a tiny part of the customer's total cost but are critical for equipment reliability.
- Failure of insulation can result in failure of the entire motor/electrical system.
- Products are qualified into customer manufacturing processes and can also be specified by OEMs.
- High cost of failure + qualification requirements + technical support = strong switching barriers.
- CY25 gross margin improved 36.9% → 38.1%, while EBITDA margin increased 19.3% → 20.3%, despite raw-material inflation.

EERM | HIGH-MARGIN MIX SHIFT
- EERM contributed only 19.4% of CY25 revenue but around 29% of segment profit.
- Higher margins make EERM an important driver of potential future mix improvement.
- Key thesis: gradually reduce dependence on conventional electrical-insulation products and increase exposure to differentiated, higher-value materials.

TECHNOLOGY & PRODUCT EXPANSION
- Started manufacturing 22 products acquired from Von Roll India, adding high-voltage resin and tape technologies.
- Absorbing global ELANTAS technologies including:
  - VOC-free unsaturated polyester resin.
  - High-voltage epoxy impregnating resin.
  - Thixotropic epoxy resin for high-voltage wind generators.
- Expands the portfolio toward more specialised electrical and high-voltage applications.

EV + BESS + POWER ELECTRONICS
- Developing potting materials and thermal-interface materials for battery systems.
- Global R&D project for a high-thermal-conductivity adhesive for BESS targeted for absorption in 2027.
- Electrification increasingly requires advanced insulation, thermal management, protection and reliability — areas where ELANTAS is building capabilities.

CAPACITY EXPANSION
- Approved ₹56 Cr Ankleshwar expansion.
- Plans to double solvent-recovery capacity.
- Working toward a new greenfield manufacturing facility at Bharuch.
- Additional capacity can support the company's expanding product pipeline.

CTC | POWER TRANSMISSION OPPORTUNITY
- CTC (Continuous Transposed Conductor) is used in high-power transformers.
- ELANTAS was able to scale CTC manufacturing within around 3 months when demand surged.
- Provides exposure to the growing transformer and power-transmission investment cycle.

THE BIGGER TRANSFORMATION
- The story is not simply:
  India electrification → more wire enamel → more revenue
- The broader evolution is:
  Core Insulation → High-Voltage Materials → Electronics → EVs → BESS → Advanced Power Transmission
- ELANTAS is attempting to move up the value chain by combining existing customer relationships, technical know-how and the global ELANTAS technology platform.

KEY THING TO WATCH
- Electrical Insulation still dominates the business.
- The key question is whether EERM and other higher-value applications can become a materially larger share of revenue and profit.
- Successful execution could reposition ELANTAS from a conventional insulation-chemical manufacturer toward a high-value materials partner for electrification, power infrastructure, electronics, EVs and energy storage.

𝗠𝗶𝗱𝗰𝗮𝗽 𝗜𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝗖𝗗𝗠𝗢: 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗴𝗿𝗲𝘄 𝟱𝟬%+ 𝗹𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝗾𝘂𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗲𝗿?

We screened Q1 FY27 (April to June 2026) results for midcap CDMO names with 50%+ company-wide revenue growth.

Short answer: the list is thin. Most CRDMO players run mixed books (API plus formulations plus contract manufacturing), project timing is lumpy, and several of the cleanest names have already moved into largecap territory.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗰𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗵𝗶𝘁

𝗡𝗲𝘂𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗟𝗮𝗯𝗼𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗼𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 (market cap around ₹25,000 crore)
Revenue up around 116 to 119% YoY to around ₹641 to 650 crore. Commercial CMS/CDMO projects did the heavy lifting, with export traction across Europe and the US. Margins expanded sharply alongside.

𝗦𝘁𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗴, 𝗯𝘂𝘁 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝟱𝟬%

𝗦𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗽𝗮 𝗠𝗲𝗱𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲 (around ₹18,800 crore): revenue up 43 to 45%. Formulations more than doubled, specialty CDMO picking up.

𝗔𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗶 𝗣𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗯𝘀 (around ₹7,800 crore): revenue up 39 to 42%, with fresh capex announced for additional capacity.

𝗜𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘃𝗮 𝗖𝗮𝗽𝘁𝗮𝗯 (around ₹6,700 crore): revenue up 34%. CDMO segment, at around 70% of the book, grew around 32%.

𝗔𝗸𝘂𝗺𝘀 𝗗𝗿𝘂𝗴𝘀 (around ₹12,000 crore): topline up 14%, core CDMO revenue up 18 to 19%.

𝗖𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗼𝗿𝗱 𝗕𝗶𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵 (around ₹16,400 crore): up 26%. API led, with CDMO ambitions.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝗳𝗶𝗹𝘁𝗲𝗿 𝗶𝘀 𝗱𝗼𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲

Laurus Labs reported CDMO revenue up around 67%, and Divi's CDMO grew around 50%. Both sit outside the midcap bucket, so they fall out of this screen even though the underlying trend is identical.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗱

The structural story is intact: China plus one, more commercial stage work shifting to India, peptides, ADCs, complex chemistry.

But one quarter tells you very little in this business. Shipment timing and the development versus commercial mix can swing a quarter hard in either direction. What matters is order book conversion, client concentration and utilisation tracked across four to six quarters, not a single YoY print.

Which midcap CDMO names are on your list that we have missed?

Aluminium conducts heat at 237 W/mK, Copper conducts at 400 W/mK (Watts per meter-Kelvin)

That is why copper gets used in high-power electronics cooling despite being heavier and more expensive. DRDO and IISc Bangalore created new composite by mixing aluminium-silicon alloy with carbon nanotubes. It reaches 335-355 W/mK, very close to copper performance. 

Aluminium holds 61% of global heat sink market because it is lighter and cheaper, If you can make aluminium perform like copper at aluminium prices, that market shifts fast

Every fighter jet, radar system, and missile carries heat sinks to cool electronics. Most of these use copper because aluminium alone cannot handle high thermal loads well enough. 

But copper weighs 3x more, which matters on airborne platforms where weight directly affects fuel and payload. IISc developed aluminium composite with carbon nanotubes for DRDO that conducts heat at 335 W/mK, near copper range.

Weight drops by 65%, cost drops further. Indian defence just moved from importing copper cooling parts to growing domestic capability in advanced thermal materials

Global thermal management market sits at $18bn in 2026 and growing at 10% per year. AI servers run GPUs that consume 600-1200 watts each, generating extreme heat in tight spaces. 

Current cooling depends on copper-aluminium hybrid heat sinks because neither metal alone works well enough at high density. DRDO-IISc composite hits 335-355 W/mK using carbon nanotubes in aluminium matrix. That is copper-grade performance at aluminium weight. 

Research was done for defence radar and missile cooling, but same properties apply directly to GPU server racks and EV battery packs.

RAYMOND LIMITED | DEFENCE × AEROSPACE × PRECISION ENGINEERING

AEROSPACE — HIGH-VALUE COMPONENTS
- 1,300+ aerospace engine parts developed with 25+ aerospace customers.
- 350+ parts developed for the latest LEAP engine variants.
- ₹5,960 Cr long-term aerospace order visibility.
- Long qualification cycles and stringent aerospace certifications create high entry barriers and switching costs.

DEFENCE — PRECISION MANUFACTURING
- Precision-machined components and assemblies for defence applications.
- Mass production of precision defence components has commenced.
- AS9100D / NADCAP ecosystem strengthens qualification barriers.
- Increasing defence localisation creates an opportunity for domestic precision-engineering suppliers.

PRECISION ENGINEERING / AUTO
- 2,000+ auto-component SKUs across ring gears, flex plates, shafts and transmission components.
- EV and hybrid platforms create a new opportunity for high-precision components.
- Precision Technology & Auto EBITDA grew ~46% YoY in Q1 FY27.
- Existing engineering capabilities provide a base for expanding into higher-value mobility applications.

THE INFLECTION
- Qualification → Customer approval → Orders → Capacity addition → Volume ramp-up → Operating leverage → Margin expansion → ROCE / FCF improvement.
- Q1 FY27 consolidated EBITDA stood at ₹100 Cr with a 15.9% margin.
- The key opportunity is the transition from a traditional engineering business toward qualification-driven, high-value global supply chains.

WHAT MAKES THE STORY INTERESTING
- The investment thesis is not simply about the Raymond brand.
- The bigger opportunity is building a strategic supplier position in global aerospace, defence and mobility ecosystems.
- Once products are qualified and production scales, long customer cycles can support sticky revenues and operating leverage.
- Higher-value product mix can potentially improve margins and capital efficiency over time.

4 NUMBERS TO WATCH
- Aerospace revenue growth.
- Capacity utilisation.
- ROCE.
- Free cash flow.

KEY TAKEAWAY
- Aerospace qualification + defence scale-up + precision-engineering growth could transform Raymond into a strategic high-value supplier, with ROCE and FCF the key proof points.

INDIAN MARKETS : FCNR FUNDRAISE CREATES LIQUIDITY & INTEREST-RATE CHALLENGE

•Large FCNR inflows have injected substantial rupee liquidity into the domestic banking system, creating a “problem of plenty.”

•RBI may need to absorb around ₹7 lakh crore of excess liquidity to prevent downward pressure on interest rates and inflationary risks.

• Highlights a potential interest-rate mismatch, with foreign funds allegedly costing ~6–7% while liquidity absorption earns around 5.5%, creating a negative carry for RBI.

•Concern is that continuous liquidity absorption, along with heavy IPO fund-raising, could reduce surplus liquidity available to the stock market.

•Major long-term risk is the redemption period over the next 2–4 years, when foreign-currency liabilities will need to be repaid irrespective of returns generated from deployment.

•Key issue is the absence of a clearly defined end-use strategy for the large foreign-currency inflows.

Impact: Negative for Market Liquidity (Large liquidity absorption and future redemption obligations could tighten domestic financial conditions and weigh on equity-market liquidity)

EXICOM TELE-SYSTEMS | TRITIUM TURNAROUND + CRITICAL POWER SCALE-UP

BUSINESS & MOAT
- Exicom operates across two key businesses: Critical Power systems for telecom sites and EV charging hardware through India operations + US subsidiary Tritium.
- Critical Power contributed ₹177 Cr in Q1 FY27, +73% YoY, while standalone EV charging revenue was ₹61 Cr, +15% YoY.
- Exicom has >50% share in India's wallbox charger market and ~60% share in the BharatNet government fibre project.
- Deep qualification cycles and switching costs support the moat; telecom customers have worked with Exicom for ~30 years.
- Consolidated order book stood at ₹1,400 Cr as of June 30, 2026.

INDIA BUSINESS — STRONGER GROWTH
- Standalone Q1 FY27 revenue was ₹234 Cr, +58% YoY, with EBITDA of ₹16 Cr.
- Standalone EBITDA margin improved to 8.8% from 5.8% YoY; gross margin was 29.1%.
- Hyderabad plant became fully operational in Q4 FY26 and triples production capacity.
- Production is shifting from Gurgaon to Hyderabad over the next 2–3 months, eliminating ₹8.7 Cr of annualised parallel-run fixed costs.
- Critical Power exports expected to rise from ~8% of sales in Q1 FY27 to ~15% by FY27-end.
- BESS is expected to scale from near-zero to ~₹50 Cr revenue in FY27, supported by 15 MWh orders already won.
- India business could compound at 20–30%, supported by telecom tower additions and EV penetration.

TRITIUM — THE BIG TURNAROUND DRIVER
- Consolidated EBITDA turned positive in Q4 FY26 for the first time since Tritium acquisition.
- Tritium is targeting 3x revenue growth in FY27 and EBITDA breakeven by Q4 FY27.
- Q1 FY27 Tritium bookings reached $20.8 Mn, around 2x the previous quarterly average; backlog was ~$20 Mn as of July 1.
- Q1 FY27 Tritium revenue was ~$10.5 Mn; 3x FY27 growth implies roughly $120 Mn annualised revenue.
- TRI-FLEX and other new products are under trials with Fortune 100 companies.
- A successful hyperscaler qualification could create a $30–35 Mn FY28 revenue opportunity per product.
- A $30 Mn firm Fortune 50 purchase order has already been secured, with deliveries beginning January 2026; a second ~$30 Mn annual RFP is advanced.
- If product trials convert, FY28 Tritium revenue could potentially exceed $150 Mn.

COST & MARGIN INFLECTION
- Hyderabad consolidation should remove parallel-run costs and improve fixed-cost absorption.
- Consolidated EBITDA breakeven is expected in Q2/Q3 FY27, while Tritium targets breakeven in Q4 FY27.
- By mid-2028, management expects Hyderabad to be fully loaded, Tritium to reach triple-digit-million-dollar revenue and consolidated EBITDA margins to reach high-single digits or better.
- If Tritium executes as guided, consolidated EBITDA could potentially reach ₹100–150 Cr by FY28.
- FY26 VRS and retention costs were largely one-offs, while current PAT losses reflect fixed-cost absorption during the scale-up phase.

ORDER BOOK & GROWTH VISIBILITY
- Consolidated order book has reached ₹1,400 Cr.
- Tritium bookings are accelerating, providing an important leading indicator for the turnaround.
- New product launches during May–July 2026 create additional FY28 upside if customer qualifications convert.
- Completed Hyderabad capex provides capacity for the next phase without requiring fresh equity dilution.

MANAGEMENT EXECUTION — MIXED RECORD
- Management had earlier guided 50% standalone revenue growth for FY26 but delivered only 19%.
- Hyderabad plant commissioning slipped from October 2025 to March 2026.
- However, consolidated EBITDA breakeven was achieved in Q4 FY26, reportedly a year ahead of the original Tritium timeline.
- August 2026 management commentary reiterated consolidated EBITDA breakeven in Q2/Q3 FY27 and Tritium breakeven in Q4 FY27.

KEY RISKS / KILL SHOT
- The biggest risk is Tritium customer qualification and product-trial conversion.
- Failure of hyperscaler trials or delays in new product launches could derail the 3x Tritium growth and Q4 FY27 breakeven targets.
- Semiconductor and copper supply-chain volatility remains a risk.
- Working capital could rise sharply through inventory and receivables.
- Consolidated debt is ~₹370 Cr, so execution must translate into EBITDA and cash-flow improvement.
- The key quarterly monitorable is Tritium bookings and progress toward the Q4 FY27 breakeven commitment.

KEY TAKEAWAY
- Tritium qualification + 3x revenue growth + Hyderabad scale-up could transform Exicom into a high-growth, profitable EV/critical-power platform.

• A dedicated financing and support mechanism could provide meaningful relief to renewable energy developers affected by grid-related curtailment, particularly by helping them service debt until transmission constraints are resolved.

DHOOT TRANSMISSION | Q1 FY27 — STRONG GROWTH + EV MOMENTUM

Q1 FY27 PERFORMANCE
- Revenue: ₹1,446.4 Cr, +49.7% YoY and +13.2% QoQ.
- EBITDA: ₹218.4 Cr, +29.0% YoY and +22.1% QoQ.
- EBITDA margin: 15.1% vs 17.5% YoY and 14.0% QoQ.
- PBT before exceptional items: ₹176.9 Cr, +39.4% YoY.
- PBT: ₹173.9 Cr, +40.3% YoY.
- PAT: ₹132.7 Cr, +37.8% YoY.

BROAD-BASED GROWTH
- India business revenue grew 53.2% YoY.
- Global business revenue grew 18.3% YoY.
- Strong growth across both domestic and international operations.
- Indian 2W/3W market growth in Q1 exceeded management expectations.
- Both EV and ICE segments delivered strong growth.

EV — KEY GROWTH ENGINE
- EV-related supplies revenue increased 79.2% YoY.
- EV components now contribute ~27% of consolidated revenue.
- Increasing electrification is benefiting both wiring-harness and non-wiring-harness businesses.
- Strong EV growth provides increasing exposure to a structural automotive transition.

MARGIN PRESSURE
- EBITDA margin declined YoY to 15.1% from 17.5%.
- Higher input/raw-material costs and labour costs impacted margins.
- Copper and other raw-material price increases are generally passed through with a time lag.
- Therefore, quarterly margins can remain volatile depending on input-cost movements and pass-through timing.

MULTILINK ACQUISITION
- Control acquired on 11 June 2026.
- Majority of consideration paid in June, with balance paid during July/August.
- Integration progressing well and expected to complete by Q3/early Q4.
- Management expects Multilink to meaningfully scale the non-wiring-harness business.
- Acquisition should strengthen Dhoot's product diversification beyond traditional wiring harnesses.

COST / BALANCE SHEET
- Depreciation & amortisation increased 13.1% QoQ due to higher capitalisation and the Multilink acquisition.
- Finance costs declined as working-capital debt continued to be optimised following the ₹ equity infusion in March 2026.
- Other income includes ₹7.59 Cr interest income from fixed/term deposits created using part of the equity infusion.

MANAGEMENT OUTLOOK
- Management remains confident of another year of strong growth.
- Robust Indian 2W/3W demand continues to support volumes.
- Electrification is driving growth across both wiring and non-wiring components.
- Key focus is completing Multilink integration and leveraging it to significantly expand the non-wiring-harness segment.

KEY MONITORABLES
- Sustainability of ~50% revenue growth.
- EV revenue growth and contribution beyond the current 27%.
- Recovery of margins as raw-material costs are passed through.
- Successful Multilink integration by Q3/early Q4.
- Scale-up of the non-wiring-harness business.

KEY TAKEAWAY
Strong auto growth + 79% EV growth + Multilink integration could sustain Dhoot's growth, while margin recovery remains key.

NTPC’s stock has corrected 20% since May 2026 & has remained largely rangebound over past three years

NTPC’s stock price movement in recent years has moved along broader investment narratives of energy security or increased power demand that have remained short-lived on the back of modest earnings growth

Recent price correction may be excessive with valuations having come off (1.5X P/B on 2027E) as improved project execution could aid earnings growth in the medium term.

NTPC’s long-term capacity targets of 151/250 GW by FY2032/37E would entail strong capex of Rs16.9 tn (43% renewable) over next decade, while under-construction capacity (35.7 GW) will help propel earnings growth in near term.

India Glycols: The demerger has changed the investment case.

India Glycols is no longer a conglomerate of chemicals, spirits, biofuels and biopharma. Post demerger, the continuing business is a focused sustainable-chemicals platform built around an unusual ethanol → bio-EO → downstream specialty-chemicals chain.

A few things stand out:
 - FY26 revenue: ₹1,164 Cr
 - Adjusted EBITDA: ₹330 Cr
 - Adjusted EBITDA margin: 28.4%
 - Bio-glycol capacity: 1.75 lakh MTPA
 - Glycol ethers/acetates: 70,000 MTPA
 - 97% renewable raw-material content
 - 100+ customers across 40+ countries
 - 51:49 JV with Clariant

The interesting part is that revenue actually declined ~26% from FY24 to FY26, while adjusted EBITDA increased ~34%.

That suggests a meaningful mix/quality improvement—but it needs to be unpacked.

The biggest opportunity could be utilisation and downstream value addition. Yet the presentation leaves an important gap: FY26 bio-glycol sales volume was only ~28,750 MT against 175,000 MTPA installed capacity.

Then there is the Clariant JV, which contributed ₹419 Cr of sales and ₹95 Cr of PAT. That validates the platform, but also means investors should not treat the 28.4% adjusted EBITDA margin as pure stand-alone operating profitability.

Management’s ₹2,000 Cr revenue / ₹400 Cr EBITDA target in 4–5 years is interesting, but I would treat it as an aspiration, not a forecast until we see the capex roadmap, utilisation, customer commitments and returns.

The demerger creates the opportunity for better price discovery.

Now the real question is:

Can India Glycols convert its renewable-carbon advantage and spare capacity into sustained specialty-chemical growth—without compromising capital efficiency?

That is the story worth tracking.

**FCNR Sugar Rush What does it means for India**
FCNR experiment has turned into a blockbuster. Total inflows exceeded $136bn vs market expectations of ~$80bn. FCNR(B) deposits alone ~$127bn
  
Like Hindi movie, climax was amazing. 
Total inflows were ~$41bn by July-end, ~$73bn by Aug 21 and ~$136bn by Aug 31. Biggest forex mobilization drives India has ever seen. August was where the real frenzy happened. FCNR deposits jumped from ~$65.4bn on Aug 21 to ~$127.2bn by Aug 31.
  
Why did NRIs rush in? RBI effectively removed the pain point: currency hedging cost. Banks offered attractive yields while RBI absorbed swap costs For investors, FCNR became a rare risk-reward opportunity. Attractive $ returns + ability to leverage deposits (leverage run 4-5x)
  
FCNR nuance: Depositor takes bank credit risk but avoids INR depreciation risk since deposits remain in foreign currency. Currency mismatch is largely handled by RBI A key incentive for banks: incremental FCNR funds were exempted from CRR & SLR requirements.
  
More deployable money, less regulatory drag hence higher NIMs, Every $ mobilized can potentially earn better spreads for banks Flip side: Liquidity is now overflowing. System liquidity has surged sharply as these inflows entered the banking system

When banks are flush with money, appetite for wholesale funding drops. That's already showing up in lower CD rates & softer short-term funding costs Excess liquidity usually pushes overnight money market rates lower. Too much cash chasing too few opportunities compress yields
 
The RBI also gets a strategic advantage. Larger forex reserves and dollar balances improve its ability to manage forward market positions & reduce pressure from speculative USD demand. Forward dollar short should be reduced going forward
 
For currency speculator, the message is important. Betting aggressively against ₹ becomes tougher when RBI has significantly larger forex ammunition and stronger external buffers Now comes the hard part. Raising $136bn is the easy part.
  
Deploying it productively is the challenge. These are time-bound liabilities with an embedded cost. Eventually the money must earn more than it costs. INR already showing strength: USDINR below 95 today
 
The success of this scheme won't be judged by the $136bn raised. It will be judged by whether India converts this liquidity windfall into stronger growth, stable ₹, lower funding stress & productive credit creation over the next few years

Good Bad & Ugly Side of Happiest Mind / ITC infotech merger Happiest Minds is merging into ITC Infotech. Promoters led by Ashok Soota will first sell a 22.1% stake to ITC for ~₹1,330 Cr at ₹390-400/share (1330cr for 22%), followed by the merger

25 shares of ITC Infotech for every 81 shares of HMinds. Post merger, ITC Ltd own ~73.4% of the combined entity while public shareholders of HMinds own ~19% This Reverse merger lead ITC Infotech listing through HMinds, creating a listed IT services platform under the ITC umbrella

Good Scale. Happiest Minds was a niche digital engineering player. Combined with ITC Infotech, it becomes part of a much larger IT franchise with 19k+ employees & 800+ customers Management targeting a US$1bn revenue run-rate by FY28.

That's a league Happiest Minds may have taken years to reach on its own For investors, this is also a migration from a MicroCap IT to a SmallCap-sized technology platform with deeper client relationships & larger deal eligibility.

Backing of ITC matters. Strong parentage, capital support, governance comfort & ability to pursue acquisitions without worrying too much about balance-sheet. Cross-selling opport looks real. HMinds brings AI, cloud, cyber security & digital engineering. ITC brings SAP, PLM etc

BAD Happiest Minds is better growth story. It was growing faster n operating at superior profitability versus ITC Infotech. Merged entity runs a risk that growth optimization gives way to scale optimization. Markets often pay premium multiples for focused specialists

Focus: Within ITC's ecosystem, how much strategic mindshare will the IT business receive compared to cigarettes, FMCG, hotels, paperboards & agri Post merger, they become minority investors inside a much larger group structure. The investment thesis changes materially.

UGLY Promoters are getting an immediate liquidity event at ₹390-400/share through the stake sale. Minority shareholders don't get that same option. Why should only promoters monetize it? Minority holders should get comparable cash exit route may be lower price for control

Happiest Minds' entire m-cap is roughly ITC can generate in a single quarter through profits/cash flows. Minority investors may feel their capital is now parked in a long-dated integration story rather than a standalone growth company

Is Pvt Banks Really Losing Share vs PSU Banks?

Everyone is talking about PSU banks taking share from Pvt banks. The narrative is simple: PSU banks are growing faster than Pvt banks, so PSU banks are winning. But the reality is a lot more nuanced.

Argument is : PSU banks are fine with 1.0-1.3% RoA vs  Pvt banks target higher profitability. Pvt banks don't want to trade-off profitability for growth.

This has impacted valuations. Premium Pvt bank multiples came with expectation of steadily MS gain vs PSU. Post-Covid, that trend has slowed, creating doubts.

If PSU banks are sacrificing yield for growth, where should it show up first? HFC, safest retail assets with low NPA, Yet PSU bank share has drifted from ~35% in FY21 to ~34% in H1FY26, while Pvt banks have inched up from ~39% to ~40%.

If PSU banks were aggressively chasing growth regardless of return, housing should have been the biggest battleground. The data doesn't show that. PSU gained initially, now plateaued. 

PSU not gainin share from Pvt banks. Market share remained stable, data also inc. HDFC merger boost for pvt bank

So where is PSU growth actually coming from? A large part is Gold Loans.

Many Pvt banks have stayed away from becoming aggressive gold lenders. The business is operationally intensive and risky. PSU banks have been far more active, esp Canara/SBIN. 

Recently, incremental industry gold loan growth has come primarily from PSU banks, increasing their dominance in banking gold-loan AUM.

Second area is Agri lending. PSU banks have stepped up agri lending. May be it’s mandate-driven, or due to deeper reach into semi-urban and rural India where Agri credit demand is.
These segments Pvt banks is not that agressive. PSU banks are gaining share at the system level. But pvt dominance continue in safe mortgages, affluent retail.

Jefferies power equipment

Many Problem: Solar led grid instability / Energy import / Pollution One solution: EV India is winning solar race. Solar supply a huge chunk of daytime power, pushing net grid demand sharply lower arnd noon. But demand peaks after sunset. That's the classic "duck curve" problem

~80 GW swing created largely by renewable output. The irony: clean power is available when demand isn't. Several states doing solar curtailment as the grid couldn't absorb all midday generation. So, next phase of green transition is tougher than just adding more solar panels

India imports ~90% of its crude oil needs & roughly half of its natural gas . Energy security remains one of the biggest economic vulnerabilities. Crude oil is among India's largest import items. Every $ oil prices widens the import bill = trade deficit = pressure on Rupee

Air pollution remains a public health emergency in major metros. Delhi frequently records PM2.5 levels many multiples above WHO norms, while Mumbai too has seen worsening air quality episodes. Solar, oil imports & air pollution are not separate challenges. They are connected

The common link is urban transport. A large share of oil consumption in metros comes from ICE cars commuting daily between home & office. Think about office parking lots. Vehicles remain parked for 8-10 hrs during the exact period when solar generation is highest

What if every major office complex became a daytime EV charging hub? Cars would consume power when solar generation is abundant, helping flatten the duck curve instead of deepening it.

Corp can accelerate this shift. EV subsidy for employees & workplace chargin infra can become part of CSR spend (2% of PBT) Vehicles in metros spend most working hours parked at offices. Converting 20%+ of parking capacity into chargers can create a daytime demand for solar power

One solution. Multiple benefits. More EVs = lower oil imports, cleaner city air, higher daytime power consumption, better solar utilisation & stable grid. Sometimes the smartest energy storage isn't a battery plant. It's millions of parked EVs connected to chargers.

Underappreciated SBI MF's distribution moat 

SBI MF's biggest advantage isn't fund performance. It's distribution. In India, bank-backed AMCs blessed with an edge as the bank branch is still the most powerful financial distribution channel
Investors trust banks with savings, salaries & FDs. Convincing a depositor to buy a bank-sponsored MF is far easier than acquiring a customer from scratch. Trust compounds over time
This trust factor is visible across the industry. 4 of India's top 5 AMCs are bank-backed. Even with rising competition, large AMCs have largely retained market share
SBI has the widest reach across the country, with one of the largest branch networks, customer bases & geographic presence among all financial institutions. That reach is difficult to replicate
Unlike most AMCs, SBI MF gets disproportionate support from its parent. SBI Bank contributes 35% of SBI MF's equity AUM. Compare that with just 8% for ICICI AMC & 6% for HDFC AMC
More interestingly, 40% of SBI MF's equity AUM comes through bank channels, versus 19% for ICICI AMC & 12% for HDFC AMC. SBI's distribution engine remains a major growth driver
Most banks operate open architecture & recommend products across AMCs based on suitability. SBI may have open architecture formally, but data suggests SBI customers get mostly SBI-branded investment products
The numbers are striking. 100% of SBI MF's promoter-bank sourced AUM sits with SBI, vs 70% for ICICI AMC & just 28% for HDFC AMC. That's about as captive as distribution gets
SBI's MF penetration opportunity is still huge. Average MF AUM per SBI branch is only ~10% of retail deposits per branch, implying a long runway for existing customers to migrate from deposits into MFs
The next leg of growth likely comes from B30 markets. SBI MF already has the highest B30 equity AUM share at 16%, ahead of ICICI AMC (12%) & HDFC AMC (11%)
SBI's deep Tier-2/Tier-3 presence matters. 66% of SBI MF's SIPs originate from B30 markets, giving it access to underpenetrated investors who are just beginning their financialization journey
The final edge is economics. SBI MF's distribution cost through SBI is just 65 bps, lower than HDFC AMC's 68 bps & ICICI AMC's 69 bps. Better reach + higher trust + lower cost = a distribution moat that's hard to disrupt

The Relationship Trump Misunderstood:
For three decades, China and emerging markets effectively exported disinflation to the developed world. They produced goods at a fraction of Western costs and shipped them to consumers in the US and Europe. The result: lower prices and higher purchasing power
The West got cheaper TVs, phones, clothes, furniture and industrial goods. China got manufacturing jobs, export growth and rising incomes. It wasn't a one-way relationship. Both sides benefited
As exports surged, China accumulated enormous foreign exchange reserves. Every dollar earned from exports added to a growing pool of savings that had to be invested somewhere
Those reserves served two purposes: protect the yuan from volatility and build strategic national wealth. China used them to buy foreign assets, resources, companies and financial securities around the world
A large portion of those reserves found their way into US Treasuries. China became one of the largest lenders to the US government, recycling export earnings back into America's financial system
This mattered because sustained Treasury demand helped keep long-term US interest rates lower than they otherwise would have been. Cheap imports lowered inflation. Treasury purchases lowered financing costs
In effect, China was helping on two fronts: suppressing goods inflation through low-cost manufacturing and supporting bond markets through reserve recycling. 
Trump focused heavily on one side of the equation: the trade deficit. From that perspective, China was exporting too much and manufacturing jobs were leaving America. This became the basis for tariffs and trade confrontation.
But the other side received less attention. Those same imports were keeping prices low for US consumers. Many products became affordable precisely because they were manufactured in lower-cost economies
The relationship also extended to capital markets. China's reserve accumulation created a steady source of demand for US government bonds, helping support the broader financial system
Today that world is changing. China is no longer a low-income economy desperate for export growth. Wages have risen, technology has improved and its economic influence is far greater than it was 20 years ago
The old model of unlimited cheap labour, ever-rising globalization and automatic reserve recycling is fading. Both countries increasingly view the relationship through a strategic lens rather than purely an economic one
As supply chains fragment and tariffs rise, the US may face more inflation from its own policy choices. Producing goods domestically or through alternative supply chains is often more resilient, but rarely cheaper
At the same time, if foreign demand for Treasuries becomes less predictable, bond investors may demand higher yields to absorb increasing government debt. Higher yields mean higher financing costs across the economy
The next decade may look very different from the last three. Less globalization, more strategic competition, potentially higher inflation and structurally higher interest rates. Markets are still figuring out what that world looks like
Bottom line: The US-China relationship wasn't simply buyer vs seller. It was a system where goods, capital and inflation dynamics were deeply intertwined. Breaking that system may create consequences on both sides.
